motivation: Tajima (with the late John Dawson, 1979) showed theoretically that an intense laser pulse drives a plasma wave whose fields exceed those of conventional radio-frequency cavities by three orders of magnitude, so that electrons can be accelerated over millimetres instead of kilometres. For decades the messy nonlinear physics of real plasmas made this look like a dream. Malka and Leemans led the experiments that made it real: Malka's group produced the first quasi-monoenergetic and then controlled-injection, tunable electron beams, and Leemans' team used plasma channel guiding to reach GeV and then nearly 8 GeV energies in centimetre-scale plasmas. Their work founded a field that now delivers compact femtosecond X-ray sources, free-electron-laser gain driven by plasma accelerators, and medical and industrial applications, and it offers a route to compact high-energy colliders. This is fundamental plasma physics turned into a transformative technology.
